item.title: Climate change also poses a threat to cultural heritage
item.description: When we talk about climate change, the debate usually centers on energy, biodiversity, carbon emissions or the economic costs of the transition. But another aspect of the problem remains largely underestimated: the impact of climate change on our cultural heritage. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fairness-based pathways shift emissions cuts while preserving global climate goals
item.description: Who cuts emissions fastest, and who supports others in doing so, are central questions in global climate action. New IIASA-led research shows that building fairness into climate models from the start can inform deliberations without changing the overall climate goal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Urban segregation study traces how history and ecology shape inequality in southern Chile
item.description: Segregation is a multidimensional phenomenon deeply intertwined with historical, social and ecological contexts. Yet this more integrated perspective has received limited attention in the Global South. A recent study focusing on the city of Valdivia offers an exception, examining three key historical moments: colonization, the devastating 1960 earthquake and current struggles to protect urban wetlands. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Five schoolgirls from Kent have built a robot to combat wildfires. Their innovative design features five-meter folding arms for clearing vegetation effectively. This remarkable achievement earned them the chance to represent Great Britain at an international robotics competition. The team will compete in South Korea, showcasing their solution to environmental challenges. They aim to inspire more girls into STEM fields through this global opportunity. item.title: New review outlines a governance roadmap for Europe's growing flood risks
item.description: In 2024 alone, flood-related disasters around the world caused more than 8,700 deaths and economic losses exceeding 450 billion euros, with cumulative global losses of about 2.7 trillion euros over the previous decade. Against this backdrop, Europe's recent floods—from riverine events in large basins to flash floods in dense urban areas—have exposed the limits of existing protection systems and emergency responses. Fuente: Phys.org.

Speaking at the opening of the Climate Week event at the United Nations in New York on Monday, the prime minister said Australians had experienced the impact of climate change up close with a series of disastrous bushfires and floods in the past decades. item.title: French farmers turn to tropical crops amid rising temperatures
item.description: In the south of France, climate change is reshaping the region’s fruit production. Rather than fighting against it, a growing number of farmers are learning how to work with it – turning to tropical crops, now well-suited to the local climate. Bananas, papaya and even dragon fruit are being grown in greenhouses but also in open fields, without heating or pesticides. Our Down to Earth team reports. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: Napa family rebuilt winery after 2017 wildfire for $30M; nine years later, $37M debt puts estate at risk
item.description: Signorello Estate winery faces an October auction after a series of devastating setbacks. The winery burned down in 2017, and rebuilding efforts faced significant delays and cost increases. Global wine sales have declined, impacting the business's revenue streams and financial stability. The owner owes $37 million to American AgCredit, which rejected a $16 million cash offer. This potential foreclosure threatens a 50-year family legacy and the jobs of ten employees. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: ‘Planetary boundaries’ necessary for flourishing of life have been massively breached, scientists warn
item.description: New report shows key indicators of Earth’s health are ‘outside the safe operating space’ as climate disaster looms The planetary life support systems relied upon by humans have deteriorated to their worst levels ever recorded amid ongoing pollution and habitat destruction, according to a key yet grim annual update by scientists. Of the nine “planetary boundaries” that help determine whether life can flourish on Earth, seven are being breached at their highest ever levels of transgression, according to the latest planetary health check, a process that was established in 2009. Continue… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Planetary Health Check 2026 finds mounting pressures across Earth's life support systems
item.description: Seven breached Planetary Boundaries continue to worsen as record ocean heat, droughts, floods, wildfires and extreme heat reveal an Earth system under strain, according to the latest Planetary Health Check. The annual update is authored by more than 60 scientists and produced by the Planetary Boundaries Science Lab at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ‘Jaw-dropping’ El Niño bursts through temperature record months before peak
item.description: ‘Godzilla-level’ phenomenon is supercharging the climate crisis and will have a huge impact on communities across the world The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months before its expected peak. The latest data shows the temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific Ocean has now reached 3.05C. That is higher than the 3.02C set in late November 2015, the previous high set in the 150 years of modern records. This temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020. Continue… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.description: British Columbia has endured another extreme drought, with damaging impacts across the province, including a watershed emergency declared by the Syilx Okanagan Nation, 70% water-use reductions for agricultural producers in Vernon, regulatory orders to protect salmon and explosive wildfires driven by severe drought conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why climate action now comes down to speed, finance and cooperation
item.description: Temporarily exceeding the 1.5°C global warming goal set in Paris is widely considered inevitable. The challenge now is to keep that overshoot as small and short as possible by cutting emissions faster, unlocking finance and strengthening international cooperation. Fuente: UN News.

item.title: La acción climática afronta su prueba más difícil: convertir promesas en resultados
item.description: Superar temporalmente el límite de calentamiento de 1,5 °C ya se considera ampliamente inevitable. El desafío ahora es evitar que la temperatura suba mucho más y permanezca por encima de ese nivel durante demasiado tiempo, reduciendo las emisiones con mayor rapidez, movilizando más financiación y aumentando la cooperación internacional. Líderes mundiales se reunirán esta semana en Nueva York, durante la Asamblea General de la ONU, para abordar estos desafíos en una cumbre sobre acción climática. Fuente: Noticias ONU.

item.title: Un escudo verde en el desierto: cómo los manglares son una defensa natural en la era del cambio climático
item.description: A diferencia de un muro de hormigón, esta infraestructura natural crece, se reproduce y puede proporcionar simultáneamente múltiples servicios. Por primera vez desde que hay registros satelitales, la superficie global de manglares ha crecido más de lo que ha disminuido, aunque el cambio climático, el desarrollo costero y la acuicultura siguen amenazando a más de 1500 especies que dependen de ellos. Fuente: Noticias ONU.

item.title: Amazon study reveals the best strategies for protecting biodiversity and carbon
item.description: A large Amazon study suggests the most powerful conservation move may be protecting the forests that are already standing. Preventing damage from wildfires and logging delivered the greatest biodiversity benefits and nearly matched deforestation prevention for protecting carbon. Restoration remains important, particularly where forests have already been heavily cleared, but it was more expensive and less effective on its own. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: ‘Incredibly encouraging’: healing the scars of traditional anchors in Dorset’s seagrass meadows
item.description: Eco-moorings help to restore seagrass in just five years, boosting sealife such as seahorses, eels and crabs One of the UK’s most precious underwater habitats – Dorset’s seagrass meadows – is recovering thanks to “eco moorings” designed to prevent the seabed being ripped up, a study has revealed. Scars caused by traditional anchors in some areas of seagrass in Studland Bay have almost entirely vanished, which is boosting the number of seahorses that thrive in the submerged meadows. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.description: The Canadian government has committed C$25m to try to rescue the caribou in the province – but there is no agreement on how best to save the keystone species The caribou of Quebec are at breaking point. The province, home to 15% of Canada’s population of woodland caribou, has seen numbers crash to about half of what they were a decade ago. For years, local First Nations people, researchers and environmental groups have criticised the provincial government’s lack of action on protecting caribou, an animal considered a keystone species by Indigenous peoples. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back to a typhoon by Tuesday morning. item.title: Children born today in Europe will live through almost twice as much extreme fire weather as their grandparents
item.description: A child born in Europe in 2025 will live through more than three additional years of extreme fire weather compared with someone born in 1950 if we continue with current climate policies, according to new research published in the journal Environmental Research Letters. That's an 84% increase for today's babies compared with their grandparents. The vast majority (86%) of this increase is due to climate change rather than increased longevity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Alabama agencies release 1,500 rare mussels into Paint Rock River after years of restoration
item.description: In an effort to revitalize the Paint Rock River's ecosystem, conservationists have introduced rare native freshwater mussels into the waters of northeast Alabama. This release is significant as these mussels are vital for filtering water and fostering biodiversity. The initiative is part of a broader commitment to preserving endangered mussel species, reflecting years of dedicated restoration work in this biodiverse watershed. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.description: People are increasingly crossing paths with the wild animals as homes ring the outskirts of forests, sparking a new era of coexistence Every year, as summer draws to a close and fall begins, California’s bears get hungry. Black bears have long roamed the state, hunting for acorns, ants and pine nuts by the bucketload to pack on calories before hibernation. But increasingly, for every berry and root, there’s an even greater temptation: our trash and the detritus of human existence. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: ‘Do you have to be dead?’: US coalminers plead for benefits as black-lung disease cases surge
item.description: Trump says he digs coal – but pneumoconiosis cases are at a 50-year high, and sick miners are mired in benefit delays For 38 years, Josh Armes worked as a coal miner in West Virginia and Virginia. After retirement, Armes, 74, of Grundy, Virginia, was diagnosed with black lung disease, medically known as coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (CWP), caused by breathing in coal dust over long periods, which irreversibly damages the lungs. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: De la sequía al diluvio: la brutal oscilación de los ríos de la península ibérica, en un mapa interactivo
item.description: El cambio climático ha traído una realidad: cada vez llueve menos en términos generales y, a la vez, cuando llueve, lo hace de forma más torrencial. Según AEMET , las regiones mediterráneas de la península y Baleares reciben ahora un 19% más de precipitación en los episodios de lluvias torrenciales que en los años 60, un patrón que la propia agencia resume así: llueve menos días al año, pero con más intensidad. Eso lo vemos y lo sufrimos con veranos más secos y diluvios inesperados, sin ir más lejos el de finales de agosto . En pocas palabras: los embalses bajan a mínimos y los ríos se secan… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Outfoxed: How well do you know your native animals? Australians’ questionable quoll knowledge exposed
item.description: About one in six NSW, QLD and Vic residents think foxes are native animals and a third believe quolls are introduced, survey shows Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Most people identify wombats and kangaroos as Australian animals, but one in six people surveyed in Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria think red foxes are native wildlife . The polling commissioned by the Invasive Species Council also revealed that one in three Australians on the east coast did not know that quolls were native. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Hurricane Hunters reveal 4 warning signs that a storm is about to strengthen
item.description: Nearly three decades of Hurricane Hunter data reveal four features that can help a tilted tropical cyclone straighten its circulation and become capable of intensifying. The findings could give forecasters an earlier warning that a seemingly disorganized storm is becoming primed to strengthen. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sea dragon populations decimated in ‘mind-blowing’ mass mortality event caused by South Australian algal bloom
item.description: Thousands of sea dragons, pipefishes and seahorses have washed up along state’s coastline according to analysis of citizen scientist records Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Thousands of sea dragons, pipefishes and seahorses died during South Australia’s devastating algal bloom, in what ecologists say is the worst mass mortality event for the fish family globally. More than 1,600 weedy and leafy sea dragons, 1,400 pipefishes and 160 seahorses washed up as the harmful algae spread… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Reactivación económica en Colombia tras el sismo: festival del pacífico viaja a Bogotá
item.description: Más de un centenar de comerciantes y portadores de tradición de la región del Pacífico en Colombia se desplazaron a Bogotá para vender productos que tenían pensados para el Festival Petronio Álvarez, una tradicional cita que no pudo darse como consecuencia del terremoto de 7,4 grados que azotó al país el pasado 10 de agosto. Esta es solo una de las tantas actividades que el Gobierno colombiano ha dispuesto para reactivar una región que desde antes del sismo ya vivía complicaciones económicas. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Rugeley Riverside Park: former power station golf course becomes wetland; 1.5km trail to open 2026
item.description: The abandoned Rugeley Power Station site is set to transform into a vibrant wetland park, focusing on the revival of natural river ecosystems and enhancing biodiversity. Visitors can look forward to a newly established walking trail that invites them to explore the reimagined landscape. This park is an integral part of a broader redevelopment plan that will include residential units and community amenities, targeted to welcome guests in September 2026. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
